stories.headline: Nobody sends a memo
stories.body:
Teams don't announce when a role has changed hands. There's no press release when a backup starts eating into the goal-line work, no chyron when a slot corner quietly becomes the plan's weak point. They just keep running the plays until the pattern is too obvious to be coincidence.

This week I found one story that cleared that bar cleanly, a couple that got most of the way there, and a couple that looked like something right up until I asked a second question of them. That second question is usually the whole job.

We'll start with the one that held up.

stories.headline: Keane didn't win the job. He just kept it after the excuse ran out.
stories.body:
The easy explanation for Dorsey Keane's goal-line takeover was sitting right there in the injury report. The incumbent was limited in Week 4, Keane picked up the extra work, and that's usually where these stories end — a role reverts the moment the starter is healthy again, and everyone moves on.

The starter came back. He was on the field, fully practicing, by Week 5. And Keane kept getting the ball inside the ten anyway — five of seven goal-line opportunities across the next two games, on top of a three-game run that took his overall share from 24% to 58%.

That's the part I find genuinely interesting. It's not that Keane got a chance. It's that the chance didn't go away once the reason for it did. Snap share and red-zone targets moved with him, not just the raw touch count, which is the kind of corroboration that turns a hot streak into a decision. The market has already started pricing it that way — his anytime-touchdown number has come in from +650 to +400.

What I can't tell you yet is whether this is a permanent handoff or an extended audition that ends the day the incumbent has one good week. Three games removed from the injury is enough to take this seriously. It isn't enough to call it settled.

stories.headline: Osei's role gave a little back, but not all of it
stories.body:
Palmer Osei's red-zone snap share tripled while Detroit's — while his team's starting tight end was out with a hamstring injury, which is unremarkable on its own. Backups play more when starters don't. The interesting part happens after the starter returns.

Osei's share came down from 34% to 26%. That's a real drop, not a footnote — whoever is telling this story honestly has to include it. But 26% is still more than double the 12% he held before any of this started, and the coordinator has been running more two-tight-end red-zone sets since the starter's return than he did in the first five weeks of the season. The market moved a little too, from +1100 to +850 — modest, matching a modest change.

I don't think this is a clean case of a job changing hands. I think it's a case where some of the gain stuck and some of it didn't, and I'd rather say that plainly than round it up into a bigger story than the evidence supports.

stories.headline: Carolina's slot problem, or somebody else's good receivers
stories.body:
Slot receivers have out-produced expectation against Carolina in two of the last three games, after sitting right around expectation for the season's first month. That's the kind of stat that wants to become a headline about a defensive weakness. I checked whether it deserved to be one.

Both of the elevated games came against receivers who rank in the league's top eight in slot production this season. The one game where Carolina held up was against a bottom-half slot receiver. That's consistent with a real coverage vulnerability. It's also exactly consistent with Carolina just having faced two good players and one mediocre one, which would mean there's no vulnerability at all.

I don't have a way to separate those two explanations from what's in front of me, and I'd rather tell you that than pick the more exciting version.

stories.headline: Keane's role, one more test
stories.body: I'm keeping Keane's file open for one reason: three games and one healthy return from the incumbent is enough to notice, but it's not enough to call a depth chart permanently rewritten. If the share holds through another game or two without a fresh excuse for it, that's a different, more settled story than the one I told this week.
